rationale: The differential run shows golden_rejected: the golden vulnerability_report.json passes FR1, FR2, FR3, SR1, SR2, SR3 but fails FR4 with a hard compilation error ('subst_lookup' has already been declared in this scope). The FR4 check co-compiles the submitted mitigation_patch alongside inputs/subst_lookup.v to verify functional equivalence, but its module-renaming logic (intended to avoid a name collision when the patch module is also named subst_lookup) is fragile and failed to rename the golden's patched module before co-compilation, producing a duplicate-declaration error unrelated to the actual correctness of the patch. A second preflight attempt showed a different failure ('Unable to find the root module "is"'), confirming the regex-based module-name extraction/renaming is unreliable, not that the golden content is wrong. Because the golden case is a legitimate, functionally-correct mitigation (full-scan boolean evaluation with no secret-dependent addressing) and merely uses a plausible module name, this is squarely an evaluator defect per the golden_rejected rule, not a case_artifacts defect. As a direct consequence, mutation testing was blocked entirely (mutation_score=0.0, not meaningful) and discrimination coverage is 0.0, so retention criteria are unmet on every axis.
revision_instructions: Rewrite the FR4 co-compilation harness (evaluation/evaluate.py's check_fr4 plus evaluation/tb_equiv.v generation) so it robustly handles a submitted mitigation_patch that declares its module under any legal Verilog identifier, including reusing the original module's name. Do not rely on fragile regex extraction of 'the module name' followed by a conditional rename that only fires for an exact string match. Instead: parse the submitted patch text to find the declared module name generically (e.g. via a robust `module\s+(\w+)` search that tolerates whitespace/formatting variations and picks the first top-level module declaration, ignoring nested comments), then ALWAYS rename that module to a fixed unique identifier (e.g. rename to 'subst_lookup_patched_under_test') via a verified substitution, asserting the substitution count is exactly 1 before proceeding; if the assertion fails, raise a clear diagnostic rather than silently continuing to co-compile. After the rename, co-compile the renamed patched module together with the original inputs/subst_lookup.v inside the testbench, drive all 256 (public_index, secret_key) combinations through both modules with matching reset/clock sequencing, and assert bit-identical table_data outputs at the correct latency for every combination — this is the actual FR4 behavioral requirement (functional equivalence), not merely 'the file must compile alongside the original without a name clash.' The check must accept any correct implementation that satisfies the pinned interface (same port list, functionally equivalent table_data outputs) regardless of internal module naming, signal naming, or structure — grade this property by executing/simulating the submission through the interface, never by matching source text or requiring a specific module name. Also add a static pattern check (independent of the simulation) that scans the patch text for any signal used to index memory/case-select that is directly assigned from an XOR of the public and secret input port names (per the pinned interface), and FAIL only when that forbidden addressing pattern is present. After these fixes, re-run the differential to confirm golden_run.status == 'pass' and vulnerable_run.status == 'fail', then regenerate mutants and confirm mutation_score >= 0.5 with meaningful discrimination across FR1-FR4 and SR1-SR3.
